title: When Computers Talk at Once

sections.title: One medium, several speakers
sections.narration: Several devices share a medium, but none can instantly know what every other device is doing. When may one transmit? This local coordination problem lies behind access protocols, and the answer begins with a collision.
sections.takeaway: Medium access control decides how stations share a communication resource.

sections.title: Make overlap visible
sections.narration: A and C start before either hears the other. Their signals overlap, making these transmissions fail. Watch the red disturbance spread. The useful question is how each station learns enough to decide what happens next.
bullets: A receiver may lose both frames
sections.takeaway: A collision concerns overlapping signals at a receiver.

sections.title: Pure ALOHA: send when ready
sections.narration: Begin with almost no coordination. Pure ALOHA lets a station send whenever data is ready. Simplicity comes at a cost: another transmission can overlap at many different starting times, forcing failed attempts to be repeated.
sections.takeaway: Pure ALOHA allows a station to begin transmitting whenever data is ready.

sections.title: A vulnerable interval of 2T
sections.narration: Let a frame last T. Another frame can interfere if it starts within T before our start, or T afterward. Slide those possibilities together: the vulnerable interval spans two T, twice the frame's duration.
bullets: Conflicts can start before or after
sections.takeaway: For equal-length pure ALOHA frames, the vulnerable interval spans 2T.

sections.title: Why retry randomly?
sections.narration: If colliding stations wait exactly the same time, they can collide again on the retry. Random waits break that symmetry. They're no guarantee for an individual attempt, but reduce the chance of repeating the same overlap.
bullets: Identical waits can repeat a clash
sections.takeaway: Independent retry timing reduces the chance of repeated collisions.

sections.title: Slotted ALOHA adds boundaries
sections.narration: Now mark shared starting boundaries. Slotted ALOHA permits transmission only at those boundaries, with frames fitting the slots. Stations can still choose the same slot, but arbitrary partial overlaps no longer create additional collision opportunities.
sections.takeaway: Slotted ALOHA restricts transmission starts to common slot boundaries.

sections.title: The vulnerable interval becomes T
sections.narration: Watch the vulnerable interval shrink. Only another attempt in the same slot conflicts with this frame. Coordinating the starts reduces the interval from two T to T, without changing the physical transmission rate.
sections.takeaway: Under the ideal slot model, the vulnerable interval is one slot.

sections.title: Interpret the ideal efficiency result
sections.narration: In the ideal model, pure ALOHA peaks near eighteen point four percent throughput; slotted ALOHA near thirty-six point eight. Push attempts past the peak and collisions dominate. More activity can actually produce less useful delivery.
sections.takeaway: The familiar ALOHA maxima depend on a specific ideal traffic model.

sections.title: Scheduling or contention?
sections.narration: There are two broad ways to organize access: assign turns, or let stations compete under shared rules. A schedule needs coordination; contention needs a way to handle conflicting attempts. Both must divide finite capacity.
sections.takeaway: Collision reduction comes with assumptions or coordination costs.

sections.title: Listen before transmitting
sections.narration: What if we listen first? Carrier sensing lets a station check whether the medium appears busy before transmitting. That information avoids some blind collisions, but a quiet local observation isn't perfect knowledge of the whole network.
bullets: Defer when the channel is busy
sections.takeaway: Carrier sensing can avoid transmissions that obviously conflict locally.

sections.title: A distant sender can still start
sections.narration: Here is the remaining problem: signals take time to travel. A distant station can start while the first signal is still approaching it. Both hear silence, both transmit, and neither has broken the listening rule.
bullets: Both ends may initially sense idle
sections.takeaway: Propagation delay allows collisions even with carrier sensing.

sections.title: One-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: One-persistent CSMA listens continuously and transmits as soon as the channel becomes idle. That eagerness limits waiting, but several waiting stations can react to the same silence together, producing another collision at the restart.
bullets: Transmit when the medium becomes idle
sections.takeaway: One-persistent stations transmit as soon as their sensed channel becomes idle.

sections.title: Nonpersistent CSMA
sections.narration: Nonpersistent CSMA waits a random interval after finding the channel busy, then checks again. Restart attempts become less synchronized. The trade-off is visible in the empty gap: everyone might still be waiting after the medium becomes free.
sections.takeaway: Nonpersistent waiting reduces synchronized attempts but can add idle delay.

sections.title: P-persistent CSMA
sections.narration: In a suitable slotted setting, p-persistent CSMA makes sending probabilistic. On an idle slot, transmit with probability p or defer. Adjusting that chance spreads competing attempts, balancing prompt use against the risk of simultaneous starts.
sections.takeaway: P-persistent CSMA makes a probabilistic choice at an idle slot.

sections.title: Add detection on historical Ethernet
sections.narration: For the next mechanism, keep one historical setting in mind: shared, half-duplex Ethernet. CSMA/CD senses before sending and detects collisions during transmission. These rules describe that shared medium, rather than every Ethernet or wireless connection.
sections.takeaway: CSMA/CD belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet, not all modern Ethernet links.

sections.title: Detect, abort, and signal
sections.narration: After detecting a collision, stop the frame, signal the collision with a jam, and back off. An unsuccessful transmission ends before wasting a whole frame. The stations then use different retry delays to separate their next attempts.
sections.takeaway: Collision detection limits time wasted on an already failed transmission.

sections.title: Why propagation affects frame length
sections.narration: A far-end collision needs time to become visible at the sender. The sender must still be transmitting when that indication returns. That's why minimum frame duration and the network's round-trip propagation delay are connected.
bullets: A far-end clash must return in time
sections.takeaway: Collision detection constrains the relation between frame time and network extent.
sections.short_title: The collision must return in time

sections.title: Widen the random retry range
sections.narration: After repeated collisions, widen the random range: two choices, then four, then eight. Binary exponential backoff gives competing attempts more room to spread. It changes the distribution of waits, rather than guaranteeing a dedicated turn.
sections.takeaway: Binary exponential backoff expands the retry-choice range after collisions.

sections.title: Work two retry choices
sections.narration: After the first collision, choose zero or one slot; after the second, zero through three. Follow the two choices in the picture. Different selections create different retry times, reducing the chance of another synchronized failure.
sections.takeaway: After two collisions, this example draws independently from four slot choices.

sections.title: Backoff does not reserve the cable
sections.narration: A completed backoff doesn't reserve the medium. Another station may already be transmitting when the wait ends. The sender still follows the channel rules. A timer tells it when to try, not that success is guaranteed.
sections.takeaway: Finishing a backoff does not guarantee exclusive access.
sections.short_title: Backoff does not reserve a turn

sections.title: Modern switched full duplex
sections.narration: Now replace the shared wire with switched full-duplex links. Separate sending and receiving paths allow opposite flows together. The old shared-medium collision mechanism no longer applies on these links, and CSMA/CD isn't used there.
sections.takeaway: Full-duplex switched Ethernet removes the shared-wire collision scenario.

sections.title: Wi-Fi needs different feedback
sections.narration: Wi-Fi faces different observation limits. A station doesn't simply detect collisions during transmission in Ethernet's way. Contention, avoidance rules, and acknowledgments help coordinate access when different stations may hear different parts of the wireless network.
bullets: Avoidance and ACKs help manage access
sections.takeaway: Wi-Fi uses collision-avoidance mechanisms rather than Ethernet-style CSMA/CD.

sections.title: Compare the added knowledge
sections.narration: Compare what each station knows. ALOHA sends; CSMA first senses; CSMA/CD also detects collisions in its shared-wire setting. Adding information changes the rules, while propagation delay still limits how quickly that information can arrive.
sections.takeaway: Each improvement adds information while retaining physical limitations.

sections.title: Explain the next collision
sections.narration: Return to the collision. Ask what each sender could hear, when it could start, and how it chooses a retry. Those three questions turn a list of protocol names into understandable responses to one shared-medium problem.
sections.takeaway: Medium-access behavior depends on both protocol rules and physical context.
